tagline: An end-to-end platform for designing, validating, producing and deploying RNAi interventions, stress-tested on Varroa destructor
summary: NECTAR is a programmable RNAi pipeline: FORAGER (computational dsRNA design with off-target screening against the Apis mellifera transcriptome), microbial production in yeast, and delivery to hives in a pollen patty. Varroa destructor, the single biggest threat to honeybees, is the first real-world case study. The team built HIVE, an explicit four-step human-practices decision procedure (Hear, Investigate, Verdict, Evaluate) run over six open project questions with 28+ named stakeholders including US EPA/FDA/USDA staff, the Chair of the UK Advisory Committee on Releases to the Environment, and the Secretariat of the Convention on Biological Diversity. Stakeholder evidence changed the chassis (living engineered Snodgrassella alvi to heat-inactivated yeast), the delivery format, the off-target screening stage, the survey instrument and the definition of success.

dry.frameworks: FORAGER, a three-stage standardised dsRNA design pipeline: target gene identification (most abundant transcripts of well-connected genes, weighted by known Varroa RNAi data), within-gene region selection (endogenous Varroa siRNA sequence features, guide competence, RNAplfold target accessibility, combined as three equally weighted complementary evidence layers rather than one fused score), and off-target analysis. Also a BEEHAVE-based colony population model and a bespoke partial-equilibrium economic model.
dry.dataviz: Hand-drawn mechanism illustrations throughout (FORAGER stages, the five-step path of a dose through the hive, the SDG goal map), a geocoded stakeholder map with latitude/longitude per interviewee, and per-cycle engineering tables; the wiki is a custom React/Astro-style build with light and dark themes.
dry.datascience: Construction of a clean Varroa destructor small-RNA dataset from public sequencing, basic population feature analysis of that sRNA pool, sequence feature analysis, whole-region homology and local exact-match screening against the honeybee transcriptome (16-nt strict mapping plus relaxed whole-region similarity), BLAST-based non-target screening, and a documented limitations table stating that the three evidence layers are equally weighted only because no Varroa RNAi efficacy data existed to fit weights.
dry.software: FORAGER is released with one file per stage and a documented frontmatter/body contract so other teams can re-run it; the HIVE method and its full interview question bank are released under CC BY 4.0. Hive insert and PCR-tube feeding adaptor are downloadable 3D-printable hardware.
techniques: RNA secondary structure and accessibility prediction
MS2 hairpin array folding optimisation (6% to 67% complete-array folding)
partial-equilibrium economic modelling with supply/demand elasticities

good.publicEngagement: Buzz In, a three-episode stakeholder podcast built deliberately to put stakeholders who disagreed with each other into contact rather than collecting views in isolation: episode 1 paired Varroa-resistance academic Prof. Stephen Martin with commercial beekeeper Paul Horton on whether to treat at all; episode 2 brought together the CEO of the Australian Honey Bee Industry Council, Amateur Beekeepers Australia and Hive & Wellness; episode 3 set the project against social, environmental and economic lenses with a social scientist, a bee researcher and an agricultural economist. GMO 101, a joint Zoom workshop with NYU Abu Dhabi iGEM on 8 October 2026, measured participation through Nearpod (24 participants, 83% took part). A beekeeper survey received a favourable opinion from a subcommittee of the Oxford Central University Research Ethics Committee (ref MS IDREC 3973787), with public task as the lawful basis and informed consent before questions; 100+ respondents, 63% reported struggling with Varroa at mean severity 5.74/10 and 70% said they would be open to a GMO-based treatment. School sessions at St Clare's summer course were run as a two-way choice exercise (present two delivery routes with honest trade-offs, ask which students would accept, measure the acceptance shift before and after) rather than a lecture. Plus street interviews, a bee campaign, Instagram and TikTok.
good.ihp: Oxford's IHP is the strongest kind: a documented decision procedure with a mandatory 'How we implemented the advice to change NECTAR' field on every one of 28+ interview write-ups, and a rule that 'We considered their feedback is not an implementation'. The largest single change is the chassis. Danny Le Feuvre (CEO, Australian Honey Bee Industry Council) and Mike Allerton (VP and Biosecurity Officer, Amateur Beekeepers Australia) both preferred a persistent living engineered Snodgrassella alvi gut symbiont because it minimises beekeeper labour; the team did not simply follow them but took the question to regulators, and Laura Bowden (GM manager, Science and Advice for Scottish Agriculture), Elizabeth Frost (NSW Department of Primary Industries), Tom Hartley (Senior Certification Officer, Soil Association Certification) and the Scottish Government Honey Bee Health Team pushed the opposite way, so the team switched to heat-inactivated, dried engineered yeast and stated plainly what that cost: the persistence that made S. alvi attractive, meaning repeat dosing and more beekeeper labour, against the preference of beekeepers they had interviewed. Austein McLoughlin of the Convention on Biological Diversity Secretariat then confirmed the inactivated product is not a living modified organism under the Cartagena Protocol, but also refused to let the team stop at SDG alignment, pushing them to ask whether NECTAR produces 'measurable improvement' - which is why the sustainability analysis widened to the whole NECTAR lifecycle and built baseline comparisons into the modelling. A joint meeting with Mike Mendelsohn and Alan Reynolds (US EPA), Adam Moyer and Laura Epstein (FDA) and Alan Pearson (USDA) then 'prevented us from treating our shift to heat-inactivated yeast as a universal regulatory shortcut', forcing jurisdiction-by-jurisdiction regulatory mapping instead of one global classification. The deepest economic chain runs through Prof. Wally Thurman (Agricultural and Resource Economics, NC State, interviewed 29 July 2026) and Prof. Brittney Goodrich (Agricultural and Consumer Economics, Illinois, 7 August 2026): Thurman set five methodological commitments (start from an average commercial operation not an industry aggregate; use existing treatments as the counterfactual; assess costs and revenues not survival rates; use simple partial equilibrium; restrict to paid pollination markets), and Goodrich's operation-level cost structure redefined the cost of Varroa to include labour, colony replacement and lost honey and pollination revenue rather than just the price of acaricide. The team then ran the chain backwards - what a beekeeper can afford, to allowable cost per dose, to allowable manufacturing cost, to required mass of intact dsRNA per gram of dry yeast - converting 'high expression' into a pass/fail wet-lab specification of 0.005 mg dsRNA per g yeast for US viability and 0.05 mg/g for both markets, against a fermentation cost of about 2.33 USD per gram. They also deliberately recruited dissent: the Oxfordshire Natural Beekeeping Group (about 20 chemical-free hobbyists) and treatment-free beekeeper Mark Sandham argued that treating removes the selection pressure that would produce tolerant bees, an argument against the entire premise; rather than abandoning the project the team narrowed its target user to commercial operations and wrote that OxNatBees changed 'not the molecular mechanism of NECTAR, but the problem we believed NECTAR should - and should not - try to solve'. Smaller but equally traceable: Lord John Krebs (first FSA Chairman) and Prof. Jim Dunwell (Chair, ACRE) made environmental fate and off-target effects explicit engineering requirements, moving non-target organisms into the FORAGER off-target screening stage and adding in vivo dsRNA-persistence experiments; Prof. Paul Lam (environmental chemistry, Hong Kong Metropolitan University) drove the adoption of BLAST off-target screening and reframed public engagement as risk management rather than promotion; Dr Michael Morrison (HeLEX, Oxford Law) rewrote the survey instrument so it asked separately about pollen patties, constitutively active engineered bacteria and inducible engineered bacteria rather than about 'GMOs' in general; Dr Théotime Colin's point about secondary pests prompted dsRNA constructs for wax moth and small hive beetle; Prof. Giles Budge's reassurance kept the adult-bee oral delivery route alive and produced the 300/500/700 bp length comparison; and Melanie Teece (Head of Technical, Hilltop Honey) and Wade Ford (Hive & Wellness) turned honey purity into a reason for additional in vivo work. The published HIVE guide names its own failure modes (interviewing agreeable people, treating 'the public' as one stakeholder, letting the Verdict drift into a summary, consulting regulators too late to change anything) and requires every Verdict to state what was decided, what was rejected and what that cost.
good.realWorld: The need is framed with numbers rather than adjectives: Varroa is an invasive alien species across most of its range and the most serious pest of the western honeybee; Australia's failed eradication attempt cost A$101 million and destroyed about 30,000 hives, and surveyed US commercial operations lost around 62% of colonies in 2024-25, estimated at over $600 million. SDGs are chosen, not collected: 15 (Life on Land) and 2 (Zero Hunger) are the primary goals with 17 and 4 as enabling goals, each mapped to named sub-targets (15.8 on invasive alien species is the headline, plus 15.1, 15.5, 15.9), and the analysis extends into the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework targets 7, 10, 11 and 17 at the CBD Secretariat's suggestion. The team then writes a dedicated negative-impacts section on goal conflicts - accessibility across economic status, pollution, ecological threat, and whether healthier managed colonies put pressure on wild pollinators (goal 15 against goal 2) - and admits an unresolved contradiction: stakeholders insisted cost was decisive while 48% of their own survey respondents ranked cost least important, with the honest line 'We have not resolved this'. Deployment rides on existing practice (dsRNA-bearing heat-killed yeast in a conventional pollen patty laid over the frames, plus a 3D-printable hive insert), the regulatory path is mapped per jurisdiction after the EPA/FDA/USDA conversation, and the cost model gives both a per-colony net private benefit and the titre threshold manufacturing must hit. They are unusually candid about what is not demonstrated: no dsRNA titre was measured against the model thresholds, the yeast could not be cloned and the E. coli route gave no detectable dsRNA, so 'this is a case for the approach, not a demonstration of the product'. Handover material - FORAGER, the HIVE cycle and question bank, the bee research guide, protocols and hardware files - is released CC BY 4.0 for future teams.

gemsTakeaway: Make the write-up template itself enforce integration: every stakeholder record must carry a 'what this changed' field, and every verdict must name what was decided, what was rejected and what that cost - then run the affordability chain backwards from what the user can pay to a numerical pass/fail specification for the bench.
